items.prompt: Which command creates a new, empty Git repository in the current folder?

options.label: `git new`
`git create`
`git start`
`git init`

rubric: `git init` initialises a repository in the current directory.
The other names sound plausible but are not Git commands.

items.prompt: Which command records the staged changes as a new commit in the local repository?

options.label: `git stash`
`git commit`
`git add`
`git push`

rubric: `git commit` saves the staged snapshot to history.
`git add` only stages, and `git push` only uploads existing commits.

items.prompt: Which command copies an existing remote repository, with its history, to your machine?

options.label: `git fetch`
`git pull`
`git clone`
`git remote`

rubric: `git clone` creates a full local copy of a remote repository.
`fetch` and `pull` need an existing local repository.

items.prompt: Which command lists the commits in the current branch's history?

options.label: `git blame`
`git diff`
`git log`
`git status`

rubric: `git log` shows the commit history.
`status` shows working state, `diff` shows changes, and `blame` shows per-line authors.

items.prompt: Which file lists patterns of files that Git should not track?

options.label: .gitignore
.gitmodules
.gitconfig
.gitkeep

rubric: .gitignore holds patterns of files Git leaves untracked.
.gitconfig holds settings and .gitmodules holds submodule paths.

items.prompt: Which commands can create a new branch named `feature`? Select all that apply.

options.label: `git checkout -b feature`
`git commit -b feature`
`git merge feature`
`git switch -c feature`
`git branch feature`

rubric: `branch`, `switch -c` and `checkout -b` all create a branch.
`commit -b` is not a valid option and `merge` combines existing branches.

items.prompt: You have just edited `app.py` in your working folder. You want it included in your next commit. Which command do you run first?

options.label: `git push app.py`
`git merge app.py`
`git clone app.py`
`git add app.py`

rubric: `git add` places the file in the staging area for the next commit.
`push`, `merge` and `clone` do not stage files.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the staging area (index) in Git?

options.label: It stores the list of branches already merged into main
It holds the changes you chose to include in the next commit
It keeps a backup copy of everything on the remote server
It holds commits that have been pushed but not yet reviewed

rubric: The staging area lets you choose exactly what goes into the next commit.
Distractors confuse it with remote backups or review queues.

items.prompt: How does `git pull` differ from `git fetch`?

options.label: `pull` only uploads commits while `fetch` only downloads them
`pull` downloads remote changes and then merges them into your branch
`pull` works on tags while `fetch` works on branches
`fetch` downloads and merges while `pull` only downloads

rubric: `pull` is a fetch followed by a merge into the current branch.
`fetch` alone only downloads and does not change your working branch.

items.prompt: What is a Git branch?

options.label: A saved set of uncommitted edits kept for later
A remote server that stores a second copy of the code
A full duplicate of the project folder stored on disk
A movable pointer to a commit that tracks a line of work

rubric: A branch is a lightweight pointer to a commit.
Distractors mistake branches for copies, stashes or servers.

items.prompt: When does a merge conflict occur?

options.label: When both branches changed the same lines in different ways
When two branches have different names for the same commit
When a merge is attempted with more than ten commits
When one branch has a file the other branch never touched

rubric: Conflicts happen when Git cannot automatically combine overlapping edits.
Files changed on only one side merge cleanly.

items.prompt: You edited a tracked file but have not run `git add`. How does `git status` describe the file?

options.label: Staged and ready to be committed
Committed and waiting to be pushed
Modified but not staged for commit
Untracked and unknown to Git

rubric: A changed tracked file that is not staged appears under changes not staged for commit.
Untracked refers to files Git has never recorded.

items.prompt: Which statements about a Git commit are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is automatically uploaded to the remote when created
It disappears from history once the file is deleted
It captures a snapshot of the staged project state
It has a unique identifier, a hash, generated from its content
It records an author and a message describing the change

rubric: Commits have hashes, authors, messages and snapshots.
Commits stay local until pushed, and deleting a file does not erase earlier history.

items.prompt: Alice and Bob both cloned a repository. Alice pushed a new commit to `main`. Bob then made a local commit on `main` and ran `git push`, which was rejected. What best explains the rejection?

options.label: Bob forgot to stage the file before running `git push`
Two people cannot clone the same repository at once
The remote has a commit Bob's local branch does not contain yet
Bob's commit message was too short for the remote to accept

rubric: The push is rejected because Bob's branch has diverged from the remote; he must pull first.
Staging and message length do not affect push acceptance.

items.prompt: What does running `git add notes.txt` do?

options.label: It starts a new branch that contains only that single file
It uploads the file to the remote repository so teammates can see it
It records a new commit containing the file in the local history
It copies the current state of the file into the staging area for the next commit

rubric: `git add` places the file's current content in the staging area; no commit is made yet.
Distractors confuse staging with committing or pushing.

items.prompt: How does `git fetch` differ from `git pull`?

options.label: `git fetch` merges remote work into your branch, while `git pull` only lists it
`git fetch` downloads new remote commits only; `git pull` also merges them into your branch
`git fetch` uploads your commits, while `git pull` downloads teammates' commits
They do the same thing, except that `git pull` only works on the default branch

rubric: Fetch only downloads; pull is fetch followed by a merge of the remote changes.
Distractors swap the directions or claim the commands are equivalent.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes a Git branch?

options.label: A movable pointer to a commit that advances when you commit while on it
A backup of the repository that is stored only on the remote server
A fixed snapshot of the project that can never change after it is created
A full copy of every project file placed in a separate folder on disk

rubric: A branch is a lightweight pointer to a commit that moves forward with new commits.
Distractors treat a branch as a file copy, a frozen snapshot or a remote backup.

items.prompt: `git status` lists `report.md` under 'Untracked files'. What does this mean?

options.label: The file is staged and has also been edited again since it was staged
Git sees the file in the folder but has no record of it in the last commit or index
The file has overlapping edits from two branches that Git could not combine
The file was in the last commit but has since been deleted from the folder

rubric: Untracked means Git has never been told to track the file.
Distractors describe conflicts, deletions or staged-then-modified files.

items.prompt: `main` has had no new commits since `feature` was created from it, and `feature` has two new commits. What happens when you run `git merge feature` while on `main`?

options.label: Git reports a conflict because both branches contain commits
Git deletes `feature` and copies its files over the files in `main`
Git creates a new merge commit that has both branches as its parents
Git moves the `main` pointer forward to the tip of `feature` and makes no merge commit

rubric: With no divergence, Git does a fast-forward by moving the pointer.
Distractors assume a merge commit or conflict is always needed.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe a merge conflict? Select all that apply.

options.label: Git inserts markers such as `<<<<<<<` into the file to show both versions
Saving the file is enough to resolve it, even if markers remain
Git silently keeps the newer commit and discards the other side's lines
Both branches changed the same lines of a file in different ways
Conflicts can only happen when pushing, never during a local merge

rubric: Conflicts arise from competing edits to the same lines and are shown with markers.
Git never silently discards changes, and markers must be removed and the file staged.

items.prompt: Priya fixed a bug, then ran `git add` and `git commit` on her laptop. Her teammate Sam runs `git pull` but does not get the fix. Priya's `git status` says 'working tree clean'. What best explains this?

options.label: Sam must run `git add` on the fix before it appears in his folder
The fix is still in the staging area and needs a second `git commit`
A clean working tree means Git discarded the commit before sharing it
The commit exists only in Priya's local repository until she runs `git push`

rubric: Commits are local until pushed to the remote.
Distractors confuse staging, committing and what a clean tree means.

items.prompt: Which command creates a new branch named `login` from your current commit and switches to it?

options.label: `git switch -c login`
`git commit -b login`
`git branch login`
`git switch login`

rubric: `git switch -c` creates and switches in one step.
`git branch login` creates without switching; `git switch login` needs an existing branch.

items.prompt: You staged `app.py` by mistake but want to keep your edits in the file. Which command unstages it?

options.label: `git restore app.py`
`git rm app.py`
`git restore --staged app.py`
`git reset --hard`

rubric: `--staged` removes the file from the index while leaving the working copy alone.
`git restore app.py` and `git reset --hard` discard edits; `git rm` deletes the file.

items.prompt: You edited `a.txt` and created a new `b.txt`. Which sequence commits only `a.txt`?

options.label: `git push origin a.txt` then `git commit -m 'Fix a'`
`git commit -m 'Fix a'` with nothing staged
`git add .` then `git commit -m 'Fix a'`
`git add a.txt` then `git commit -m 'Fix a'`

rubric: Only staged changes are committed, so stage just `a.txt`.
`git add .` would also stage `b.txt`; committing with nothing staged records nothing.

items.prompt: During `git merge feature`, `style.css` shows conflict markers. You edit it to the correct final content and delete the markers. What is the next step?

options.label: `git push --force` to publish the corrected file
`git add style.css` then `git commit` to finish the merge
`git merge --abort` to keep the corrected file
`git branch -d feature` to mark the conflict resolved

rubric: Staging the resolved file and committing completes the merge.
Abort undoes the merge; force-pushing or deleting the branch does not resolve anything.

items.prompt: You created a local branch `fix-nav` and want to publish it to `origin` and link it for future pushes and pulls. Which command does this?

options.label: `git pull -u origin fix-nav`
`git push -u origin fix-nav`
`git fetch -u origin fix-nav`
`git push fix-nav origin`

rubric: `git push -u origin <branch>` publishes the branch and sets its upstream.
Other options have wrong verbs or argument order.

items.prompt: You edited a tracked file but have not staged anything. Which commands display the changed lines? Select all that apply.

options.label: `git diff HEAD`
`git log --oneline`
`git status`
`git diff`
`git branch -v`

rubric: `git diff` and `git diff HEAD` show line-level changes against the index or last commit.
`git status` lists file names only; log and branch show commit summaries.

items.prompt: You are on `feature` with two commits. Teammates have since added new commits to `main`, and you want those changes in `feature` without altering `main`. Your working tree is clean.

options.label: `git push origin main` then `git switch feature`
`git switch main` then `git merge feature`
`git branch -d main` then `git merge main`
`git switch feature` then `git merge main`

rubric: Merging `main` while on `feature` brings main's commits into feature only.
The reverse merge changes `main`; pushing or deleting `main` does not bring in changes.

items.prompt: You made two commits directly on local `main` that belong on a new branch. Nothing has been pushed. Which sequence moves them to `fix` and puts `main` back where it was?

options.label: `git branch fix` then `git reset --hard HEAD~2`
`git stash` then `git branch fix` then `git stash pop`
`git checkout -b fix` then `git revert HEAD~2`
`git reset --hard HEAD~2` then `git branch fix`

rubric: Creating `fix` first keeps a pointer to the two commits, then the reset moves `main` back.
Resetting first leaves `fix` at the old tip, and revert or stash do not move commits between branches.

items.prompt: `feature` was branched from `main`, and `main` has had no new commits since. You run `git switch main` then `git merge feature`. What happens?

options.label: A merge commit with two parents is always created
Fast-forward: the `main` pointer moves to the tip of `feature`
Nothing changes until you run `git rebase` on `main`
A conflict is reported because both branches changed files

rubric: When `main` is an ancestor of `feature`, Git simply moves the pointer forward without a merge commit.
Distractors assume merges always create a commit or conflict.

items.prompt: A bad commit `abc123` is already pushed to shared `main`, and teammates have pulled it. Which action undoes its effect without rewriting shared history?

options.label: `git rebase -i abc123~1` to drop it, then force push
`git revert abc123` then a normal `git push`
`git commit --amend` on the latest commit, then push
`git reset --hard abc123~1` then `git push --force`

rubric: Revert adds a new commit that inverts the change, so history stays intact for teammates.
Reset, amend and rebase rewrite history and would force teammates to reconcile diverged copies.

items.prompt: You are on `feature` with 3 commits, and `main` has gained 2 new commits since you branched. You run `git rebase main`. What is the result?

options.label: `main` gets your 3 commits and 2 commits are merged in
The 2 new `main` commits are copied under your 3 commits
`feature` commits are replayed on `main`'s tip with new hashes
A single merge commit is added on top of `feature`

rubric: Rebase replays your commits onto the new base, which creates new commits with different hashes.
Other options confuse rebase with merge or reverse which branch moves.

items.prompt: During `git merge main`, Git reports a conflict in `app.py`. You have edited the file and removed all conflict markers. What is the next step to finish the merge?

options.label: `git merge --abort` to save the edited file
`git add app.py` then `git commit` to conclude the merge
`git push` directly so the remote records the resolution
`git stash` to store the file, then `git merge --continue`

rubric: Staging the file marks it resolved, and committing completes the merge.
Abort discards the merge, and pushing or stashing does not conclude it.

items.prompt: You staged some edits with `git add` and want to see exactly what is staged but not yet committed. Which commands show that? Select all that apply.

options.label: `git diff`
`git log -p`
`git diff --staged`
`git diff --cached`

rubric: `--staged` and `--cached` are synonyms that compare the index to HEAD.
Plain `git diff` shows only unstaged changes, and `git log -p` shows past commits.

items.prompt: Your team keeps a `release` branch for a shipped version. A bug fix, commit `a1b2c3`, was made on `main` alongside several unfinished features. The release needs only that fix. What should you do?

options.label: `git switch release` then `git merge main` to bring the fix
`git switch main` then `git rebase release` to share the fix
`git switch release` then `git reset --hard a1b2c3`
`git switch release` then `git cherry-pick a1b2c3`

rubric: Cherry-pick copies just that one commit onto the release branch.
Merging brings the unfinished features, and reset or rebase would move or rewrite the wrong branch.

items.prompt: `git push` is rejected with 'non-fast-forward'. A teammate pushed to the same branch an hour ago. What is the most accurate diagnosis?

options.label: Your local branch has no commits ahead, so nothing can be pushed
The remote branch has commits yours lacks, so pushing would discard them
Your credentials lack write access, which Git reports this way
Your local branch name differs from the remote, so history cannot match

rubric: Non-fast-forward means the remote tip is not an ancestor of your branch, so you must integrate first.
Other options blame permissions or naming, which produce different errors.

items.prompt: You made one local commit on `main`. After `git pull`, `git log` shows a new 'Merge branch main of origin' commit you did not write. Why did it appear?

options.label: The remote history was rewritten, so Git recorded the rewrite as a merge
Pull always creates a merge commit, even when you have no local work
Git detected a conflict and auto-created a merge commit to record it
Local and remote `main` had diverged, so pull's merge step combined them

rubric: Pull is fetch plus merge, and diverged histories need a merge commit unless you rebase.
With no local commits pull fast-forwards, and conflicts do not create merge commits on their own.

items.prompt: You ran `git checkout v1.2`, made two commits, then ran `git switch main`. The commits no longer appear in `git log` on any branch. What explains this?

options.label: The commits were stashed automatically and must be popped to return
The commits were made on a detached HEAD, so no branch pointed to them
Switching branches deletes all commits made since the last push
Tags are read-only, so Git rejected both commits on `v1.2`

rubric: Commits on a detached HEAD have no branch reference, so they are only reachable via the reflog until pruned.
Git does not delete commits on switching, tags do not block commits, and nothing is stashed.

items.prompt: A teammate rebased shared branch `dev` and force-pushed. You pull, and your log now shows each of their old commits twice. What is the cause?

options.label: Pull cannot handle rewritten history, so it copies every commit twice
Rebasing created new hashes, so your old copies merged with the new ones
Your clone is corrupt and needs a fresh `git clone` to repair
Force-push duplicates commits on the remote whenever it is used

rubric: Rebased commits have new hashes, so your local originals and the rewritten ones look like different commits to the merge.
The duplication comes from history mismatch, not corruption or a pull defect.

items.prompt: `git revert <sha>` on a merge commit fails with 'is a merge but no -m option was given'. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: Merge commits are immutable, so Git blocks reverts on them entirely
The working tree is dirty, and Git requires it to be clean for merges
The merge has two parents, and Git cannot tell which side is the mainline
The merge was already reverted, so Git refuses to undo it again

rubric: A merge has multiple parents, so `-m 1` tells Git which parent to treat as the mainline to revert to.
The error is about parent ambiguity, not immutability or a dirty tree.

items.prompt: You added `config.local` to `.gitignore`, but `git status` still shows changes to it. Which statements are correct about why and how to fix it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ignore rules apply only after the remote has pulled the `.gitignore` file
The file was already tracked, and ignore rules affect only untracked files
`.gitignore` takes effect only after you run `git add -f` on the file
`git rm --cached config.local` untracks it while keeping the file on disk

rubric: Tracked files stay tracked regardless of ignore patterns until removed from the index.
The `git add -f` and remote-sync claims are false, since ignore rules are local and read at once.

items.prompt: `feature` was merged into `main`, then a bug was found and the merge was undone with `git revert -m 1 <merge>`. After more fixes on `feature`, you merge it into `main` again, but the original feature changes do not return. What explains this?

options.label: Reverting a merge deletes the `feature` branch and its commits
Merges only apply once per branch, so Git skips the second one
Git treats the original commits as merged, and the revert removed their effect
The second merge hit a conflict that Git resolved by dropping changes

rubric: The revert commit undoes the content, but history still records the feature commits as merged, so only new commits come in.
The distractors invent branch deletion, conflicts or a once-only rule; reverting the revert restores the changes.

items.prompt: You rebased your pushed feature branch onto `main` and force-pushed. A teammate who had pulled the old branch now runs `git pull` and sees many duplicated commits. What best explains this?

options.label: The rebase copied main's commits into the feature branch, so main's own commits now show up a second time in the log
Force-push appends your new commits to the remote without removing the old ones, so the remote stores every commit twice
Rebase rewrote your commits as new ones with new hashes, so their old copies and your new ones both appear after the pull
Git pull fetches every commit twice after a force-push and removes the duplicates only when the teammate pushes next

rubric: Rebase creates new commits with different hashes; the teammate's pull merges their old versions with the rewritten ones.
Distractors misread force-push or pull as duplicating objects, or blame main's commits.

items.prompt: `git bisect` reports a merge commit as the first bad commit, yet both of its parents test as good. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Bisect cannot judge merge commits reliably and always blames the wrong one, so the parents should be retested
One parent was marked good by mistake, so the real culprit is an older commit before the merge base
The merge commit's own message holds the change that broke the build, since merges carry no file content of their own
The bug comes from how the two branches' changes interact once combined, though neither side is faulty alone

rubric: Both parents good and the merge bad points to an interaction between the two sets of changes.
Distractors blame the tool, a mislabelled parent, or the commit message.

items.prompt: `git revert abc123` fails with 'commit abc123 is a merge but no -m option was given'. Why does Git need `-m`?

options.label: Merge commits are immutable once pushed, so Git refuses to create any commit that would reverse one without an override
The revert needs the merged branch to still exist, and `-m` names that branch so Git can look up its tip
The merge had conflicts resolved by hand, and Git cannot reverse a hand-edited resolution unless told to trust it
The merge has two parents, so Git cannot know which side is the mainline to return to unless you name one

rubric: A merge has multiple parents; `-m 1` picks the mainline parent so the diff to undo is defined.
Distractors invent immutability, conflict-resolution, or branch-lookup rules.

items.prompt: Merging `feature` into `main` finishes with no conflicts, yet tests fail on the result. Both branches passed tests on their own. Which cause fits best?

options.label: Git silently dropped one branch's edits because both branches touched the same file, even in different regions
The merge used the `ours` strategy by default, so feature's changes were discarded before the tests ran
A semantic conflict: edits in separate regions were each valid but rely on assumptions the other branch changed
Tests on a branch run against cached builds, so any merge invalidates earlier results and forces failures

rubric: Textually clean merges can still be logically incompatible; only tests reveal this.
Distractors assume Git loses edits or defaults to `ours`, which it does not.

items.prompt: `main` has advanced since you branched `feature`. You want to see only what `feature` changed since it diverged. Which command does that, and why?

options.label: `git diff main...feature`, because it compares feature against the merge base, not main's current tip
`git diff feature..main`, because that order restricts output to the changes made on feature since branching
`git diff main feature`, because it compares only the commits unique to feature and ignores main's new work
`git diff HEAD~1`, because one step back always marks the point where feature diverged from main

rubric: The three-dot diff uses the merge base, isolating feature's own changes.
Two-dot forms include main's newer changes as differences.

items.prompt: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~3` on a local branch and now need the work back. Which statements about recovery are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.label: The three commits are deleted immediately, so only a remote copy of them could restore the work
Uncommitted edits to tracked files that the reset overwrote generally cannot be recovered through the reflog
The three commits stay in the object database until garbage collection prunes unreachable objects
`git reflog` still lists the earlier branch tip, so you can reset back to it
Reflog entries are stored on the remote, so recovery works only if the commits were already pushed

rubric: The reflog and unpruned objects allow recovery of committed work, but uncommitted changes discarded by --hard are lost.
Distractors treat reset as instant deletion or the reflog as remote data.

items.prompt: You rebase a 12-commit branch onto `main`. Git stops at commit 3 with a conflict in `config.yml`; you resolve it, and commits 4, 5 and 7 conflict on the same lines again. A plain merge would have shown one conflict. What best explains the repetition?

options.label: Rebase treats the branch as unrelated to `main`, so it compares every file from scratch for each replayed commit
Rebase replays commits one at a time, so each commit touching those lines must be reconciled against the new base separately
Conflicts in rebases are reported once per remote-tracking branch, and this branch has several of them configured
Your first resolution was stored incorrectly, so Git rejects it and asks for the same fix on each later commit

rubric: Rebase applies each commit in turn, so repeated edits to the same lines conflict repeatedly; squashing or rerere reduces this.
Distractors invent storage errors or remote-tracking behaviour.

items.prompt: Four developers have based work on the shared `integration` branch, and `main` has new fixes you need there. Criteria: do not disrupt their existing clones, and keep existing commits intact. Which approach is best?

options.label: Squash all of `integration` into one commit on top of `main`, because a single commit is simplest to review
Delete and recreate `integration` from `main`, because a fresh branch means no conflicts can arise later
Rebase `integration` onto `main` and force-push, because a linear history is easier for everyone to follow
Merge `main` into `integration`, which adds a merge commit without rewriting commits others already hold

rubric: Merging preserves existing commit hashes, so teammates' clones stay compatible.
Rebase, recreation and squash all rewrite shared history and break others' work.

items.prompt: A buggy commit reached `main` 20 minutes ago and three teammates have already pulled it. Criteria: fix quickly, do not break their clones, keep an honest history. Which action is best?

options.label: Delete `main` on the remote and push a clean copy, because teammates can simply re-clone the corrected branch
Run `git revert` on the commit and push, because a new undoing commit needs no rewrite of shared history
Amend the bad commit and force-push, because the fix then lives in the original commit and nothing looks wrong
Run `git reset --hard HEAD~1` and force-push, because deleting the commit leaves the cleanest history for everyone

rubric: Revert is non-destructive and safe once others have pulled the commit.
The other options rewrite or destroy shared history, forcing teammates to repair their clones.

items.prompt: A game team commits 200 MB texture files that change weekly, and clones now take 40 minutes. Criteria: keep one repository, speed up clones, keep the normal Git workflow for code. Which option is best?

options.label: Squash texture commits weekly, because fewer commits means Git stores fewer full copies of each binary
Run `git gc --aggressive` weekly, because compressing the repository shrinks binary history to near zero
Track the textures with Git LFS, so clones fetch small pointers and download file content on demand
Add the texture folder to `.gitignore`, because ignored files stay versioned but are left out of clones

rubric: LFS keeps large binaries out of regular history while staying in one repo.
Compression and squashing barely help changing binaries, and .gitignore stops versioning entirely.

items.prompt: A push to a shared feature branch is rejected as non-fast-forward because a teammate pushed first. A colleague proposes `git push --force`. Which critique is most sound?

options.label: It is fine on any branch except `main`, so it is the standard way to resolve rejected pushes on feature branches
It would overwrite the teammate's commits; fetch and integrate first, or at least use `--force-with-lease`
It would merge the remote's new commits into yours automatically, so the rejection disappears without losing anything
It would fail anyway, because Git forbids forced pushes to any branch that has more than one contributor

rubric: Plain force discards remote commits you have not seen; integrating first or --force-with-lease protects them.
Distractors claim force merges work, is always safe off main, or is blocked by Git.

items.prompt: Team policy: `main` must stay linear, each pull request must be revertible with one command, and intermediate 'wip' commits have no value. Which PR merge method best fits?

options.label: Fast-forward only, because it keeps the branch commits and a single revert removes the whole PR
Merge commit, because it preserves every wip commit and lets the whole PR be reverted at once
Rebase and merge, because it replays every wip commit linearly and one revert undoes all of them
Squash merge, because each PR becomes one commit, so main stays linear and a revert undoes the whole PR

rubric: Squash merge yields one linear commit per PR, which can be reverted with a single command.
Other methods keep wip commits, and reverting them takes several commits or a merge-parent choice.

items.prompt: An API key was committed and pushed to a shared repository's feature branch two days ago; it may already have been copied. Which actions are necessary for a sound response? Select all that apply.

options.label: Commit a deletion of the file, because later commits hide the key from anyone who clones the repository
Revert the commit that added the key, because a revert removes it from every earlier commit in history
Purge the key from all history with a history-rewriting tool, then force-push the rewritten branches
Tell collaborators to re-clone or rebase onto the rewritten history so they do not push the key back
Revoke and rotate the key, since anyone who cloned the repository may still have it

rubric: Rotation limits damage, history rewriting removes the secret, and collaborators must resync to avoid reintroducing it.
Deleting or reverting only changes the latest tree; the key stays in earlier commits.

items.prompt: A 30-developer team ships weekly. Feature branches live about three weeks, and every merge brings painful conflicts and late integration bugs. Criteria: fewer conflicts, continuous integration, and unfinished work must not reach users. Which workflow fits best?

options.label: Give each developer a personal fork and merge forks only at release, because isolation prevents conflicts from forming
Freeze `main` for two days before each release, because a freeze lets the long-lived branches integrate calmly
Trunk-based development with short-lived branches merged daily and unfinished features hidden behind flags
Keep long-lived branches but merge `main` into them monthly, because less frequent merging means fewer conflicts

rubric: Frequent small merges reduce conflict size, and flags keep incomplete work hidden from users.
Other options delay integration, which grows conflicts rather than reducing them.

items.prompt: A feature branch has been pushed and three colleagues have built work on top of it. Main has moved ahead and you want to bring those changes in. Criteria: don't disrupt colleagues' work, keep the update safe. Which approach is best?

options.label: Merge main into the branch, because rebasing would rewrite commits that three colleagues already based work on
Squash the branch into one local commit, because that avoids any divergence from the shared remote branch
Rebase and push normally, because Git reconciles rewritten commits automatically on each colleague's next pull
Rebase the branch onto main, because a linear history outweighs the risk of colleagues diverging from the rewritten commits

rubric: Merging adds commits without changing published ones, so colleagues' work stays valid.
Distractors assume rebasing shared commits is harmless or that Git auto-reconciles rewritten history; it does not.

items.prompt: Commit abc123 on main introduced a bug. It was pushed two hours ago and 12 developers have already pulled it. Criteria: do not rewrite shared history, keep an audit trail. Which undo is best?

options.label: `git reset --hard abc123~1` then `git push --force`, because it removes the bad commit from every clone's history cleanly
`git rebase -i abc123~1` to drop the commit then push, because dropping it preserves everyone's local clones untouched
`git commit --amend` on the newest commit, because amending retroactively fixes the earlier commit for all clones
`git revert abc123` and push, because it adds an inverse commit and leaves existing history intact

rubric: Revert is the non-destructive undo for published history.
Reset, rebase and amend all rewrite history that others already hold, which breaks their clones.

items.prompt: After rebasing your feature branch locally, you must update the already-pushed remote branch, which a colleague occasionally pushes to. Criterion: minimise the chance of silently overwriting their commits. Which push is best?

options.label: `git push --force`, because it checks the remote tip first and aborts if a colleague pushed in the meantime
`git push --no-verify`, because skipping hooks stops the remote from accepting concurrent updates over yours
`git push --force-with-lease`, because it refuses when the remote branch has moved beyond what you last fetched
`git push --follow-tags`, because it fast-forwards the remote even when your local history was rewritten

rubric: force-with-lease compares the remote ref to your last-known value and aborts if it differs.
Plain --force performs no such check; the other flags do not address rewritten history.

items.prompt: Team criteria for merging topic branches: every commit builds and passes tests, `git bisect` must be able to pinpoint a small change, and authorship per commit is kept. Which merge strategy fits best?

options.label: A `--no-ff` merge, because the branch's atomic commits stay reachable so bisect can isolate the exact change
A squash merge, because one commit per feature lets bisect isolate the exact change inside that feature
Cherry-picking only the final commit, because bisect needs just the end state of the branch to find regressions
A squash merge, because squashing keeps each original commit as a separate reachable entry for bisect to test

rubric: Preserving the atomic commits gives bisect fine granularity and per-commit authorship.
Squash collapses the commits into one, losing the granularity the criteria require.

items.prompt: A developer committed an API key, then removed the file in the next commit and pushed to a public repository. They propose that this resolves the leak. Which assessment and response is best?

options.label: Run `git gc --prune=now` on the remote clone, because it permanently erases unreachable commits from every fork
Force-push a cleaned history and skip rotation, because rewritten history makes the leaked key unusable to others
Revoke and rotate the key first, then optionally purge history, because anyone who cloned already holds the old commit
Deleting is enough, because the file no longer appears in the branch tip that people normally check out

rubric: A secret in public history must be treated as compromised; rotation is the real fix.
Distractors assume deletion or history rewriting un-leaks a secret that copies and forks may still hold.

items.prompt: A team keeps feature branches alive for months, merging main in periodically. Which are valid drawbacks of this practice? Select all that apply.

options.label: Textual conflicts accumulate and grow harder to resolve the longer the branch diverges
Reviewers face one huge diff, which lowers review quality and delays feedback
A clean textual merge can still break behaviour when both sides change related logic in different files
Git loses track of renamed files once a branch is older than a few weeks
Git must re-store every file on each commit, so repository size grows with branch age

rubric: Divergence, semantic conflicts and oversized reviews are real costs of long-lived branches.
Git stores deltas and content efficiently, and rename detection does not depend on branch age.

items.prompt: Branch `release/1.4` holds a security fix commit H plus commits V1 and V2 that bump the version and edit the 1.4 changelog. Main needs H but must not receive V1 or V2. The team wants a traceable link from the copy back to the original. Which action is best?

options.label: Copy the changed files by hand from the release branch, because that avoids duplicate hashes and keeps history identical
`git merge release/1.4` into main, because merging brings the fix and Git skips the version-only commits automatically
`git rebase release/1.4` on main, because replaying main onto it keeps the fix and drops the version-bump commits
`git cherry-pick -x H` on main, because it copies only that change and records the source hash in the message

rubric: Cherry-pick -x takes a single commit and annotates its origin.
Merge and rebase bring V1 and V2 along; manual copying loses the traceable link.

items.prompt: A 200MB binary was committed eight months ago and the repository used by 30 contributors is bloated. Constraints: the blob must vanish from all history, and stale copies must not be reintroduced. Which plan meets both?

options.label: Rewrite with filter-repo, force-push main only, and let contributors pull so their old branches reconcile automatically
Rewrite with `git filter-repo --path big.bin --invert-paths`, force-push all refs, and have everyone re-clone instead of merging old branches
Run `git rm big.bin`, commit and push, then run `git gc` locally so the blob drops out of the shared history
Add `big.bin` to `.gitignore` and push, because ignored files are purged from earlier commits on the next fetch

rubric: The blob exists in old commits, so history must be rewritten on all refs and clones refreshed.
Removing the file or ignoring it leaves history untouched; pulling old branches can reintroduce the blob.

items.prompt: Your latest local, unpushed commit mixes a refactor and a bug fix in the same files. You need two separate commits. Which sequence achieves this?

options.label: `git reset HEAD~1`, then `git add -p` and commit the refactor hunks, then commit the rest; mixed reset leaves changes unstaged
`git reset --soft HEAD~1`, then `git add -p` to choose hunks; soft reset leaves every change unstaged for selection
`git reset --hard HEAD~1`, then `git add -p` and commit each part; the working tree still holds the changes afterward
`git revert HEAD`, then `git cherry-pick -p HEAD` for each part; revert keeps the originals available to pick from

rubric: A mixed reset moves the branch back but leaves changes unstaged, so hunks can be staged selectively.
--hard discards the changes and --soft leaves everything staged, so neither allows splitting.

items.prompt: A three-week feature branch is rebased daily onto main and hits the same conflicts every time. Constraint: reuse earlier manual resolutions automatically without changing the history shape. Which setup fits?

options.label: Rebase with `-X ours main`, because that prefers the feature branch's side for every conflicting hunk during a rebase
Enable `rerere.enabled`, because Git records resolutions and replays them when identical conflicts recur in later rebases
Set `merge.conflictstyle diff3`, because it stores earlier resolutions and applies them automatically on the next rebase
Run `git merge -s ours main` daily, because it auto-resolves conflicts by combining both sides' changes line by line

rubric: rerere (reuse recorded resolution) is designed for repeated identical conflicts.
`-s ours` discards main's changes, `-X ours` in a rebase favours upstream, and diff3 only changes marker display.

items.prompt: Design enforcement for main with these constraints: no direct pushes, linear history, passing tests required, and nothing a developer's misconfigured laptop can bypass. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: A team convention document plus `commit-msg` hooks, since developers who read it will configure their clones the same way
Setting `receive.denyNonFastForwards` alone, since it blocks direct pushes and also runs the test suite before accepting
Server-side branch protection requiring pull requests, passing status checks and linear history, since client hooks can be skipped or missing
A `pre-push` hook committed to the repo, since every clone installs it automatically and enforces the rules locally

rubric: Only server-side rules apply to every pusher regardless of local setup.
Hooks in the repo are not auto-installed, conventions are unenforced, and denyNonFastForwards does neither pushes-blocking nor testing.

items.prompt: A regression lies somewhere in 400 commits; v2.0 is good and HEAD is bad. Some intermediate commits fail to compile. Design an automated search that still finds the first bad commit. Which design is correct?

options.label: `git bisect start HEAD v2.0` then `git bisect run ./check.sh`; the script exits 0 for bad, 1 for good, and 125 when the build fails so it is skipped
`git bisect start HEAD v2.0` then `git bisect run ./check.sh`; the script exits 0 for good, 1 for bad, and 125 when the build fails so the commit is skipped
`git bisect run ./check.sh` where any build failure exits 1 so it counts as bad, since the first bad commit is still found reliably
`git bisect start HEAD v2.0` then `git bisect run ./check.sh`; the script exits 0 good, 1 bad, and 130 when the build fails so it is skipped

rubric: bisect run treats 0 as good, 1-127 (except 125) as bad, and 125 as skip.
Swapped codes invert the search; codes above 127 abort it; counting build failures as bad can misidentify the culprit.

items.prompt: A `git rebase main` on your feature branch has completed, and you now see it dropped three commits by mistake. No other Git operation has run since. Which actions restore the pre-rebase tip? Select all that apply.

options.label: `git rebase --abort` to undo the completed rebase
Find the old tip hash with `git reflog`, then create a branch at it with `git branch rescue <hash>`
`git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` on the feature branch
`git gc --prune=now` to bring back unreachable commits
`git checkout -b rescue ORIG_HEAD`

rubric: The reflog and ORIG_HEAD both still point to the pre-rebase tip, so any of them can recover it.
gc --prune=now destroys unreachable commits, and --abort only works while a rebase is in progress.

items.prompt: A team moves a repository to a new host. The proposed plan: `git clone <old-url>`, `git remote add new <new-url>`, then `git push new main`. They need every branch and tag preserved on the new host. What is the plan missing?

options.label: Cloning with `--mirror` and pushing with `--mirror`, since a plain clone and one-branch push leave other branches and tags behind
Rewriting author emails with filter-repo, since the new host rejects commits made under identities it does not know
Deleting the old remote's data first, since two hosts holding the same history would conflict with each other
Running `git gc --aggressive` before pushing, since objects that remain unpacked are not transferred to another remote

rubric: Pushing only main omits other branches and tags; mirror clone and push transfer all refs.
Packing, identity rewriting and deleting the old remote are unnecessary for migrating refs.
